sections.title: 1. EBM Principles — Literature Search & Question Formulation

blocks.text: A complete literature search must use multiple databases (not just one), cross-check the reference lists of retrieved studies, hand-search unindexed material, write to experts about missing studies, and include grey literature (conference abstracts/posters) — excluding conference posters as 'not peer reviewed' is the wrong strategy.

blocks.forTopic: Literature search completeness checklist (systematic review search strategy)
expansion: Search the reference lists of retrieved papers
Extend to papers in other languages

blocks.text: Mixing study designs (e.g. 12 uncontrolled trials + 3 RCTs) weakens rather than prevents a meta-analysis; best practice is to run two separate meta-analyses (one per design) rather than pooling heterogeneous designs together.
**PICO** format structures a treatment question as Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome; useful for treatment questions but may not fit every clinical question.
**PECO** is the equivalent structure for exposure/aetiology questions: Patient, Exposure, Comparison, Outcome.

blocks.title: The 4 Steps of Evidence-Based Practice
rows: Track down the best available evidence
Apply the evidence by integrating it with clinical expertise and patient values

blocks.text: When framing a question about a side effect (e.g. sexual dysfunction on **fluoxetine**), the most meaningful comparator population is patients not taking the drug at all, not patients on an alternative drug — this is what makes the risk figure meaningful to the patient.
Impact factor is a journal-level (not article-level) metric: it is calculated over a rolling three-year period as the average number of citations per published paper.

Cochrane Library = Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews + Database of Abstracts of Reviews of Effectiveness (**DARE**, quality-appraised reviews published elsewhere) + Cochrane Controlled Trials Register (**CENTRAL**); it is not an alternative to Medline, and not every intervention trial is registered in it.
**CENTRAL** (the Cochrane trials register) is currently the best single resource for locating registered clinical trials, including ongoing/unpublished ones.
The single most important conflict of interest a researcher reviewing a drug must disclose is receiving honoraria for lecturing from a company that makes a competing drug.

items.text: Meta-analysis pooling 12 uncontrolled trials + 3 RCTs: the trap answer is that mixing designs makes a meta-analysis impossible. Correct: it only weakens it — best practice is two separate meta-analyses.
Impact factor is tested as if it measures the quality of a specific article — it is actually a journal-level, 3-year rolling citation average.
When framing a **PICO** comparator for discussing a side effect with a patient, the trap distractor is an alternative drug; the correct comparator is 'not taking the intervention at all'.
Candidates over-trust the Cochrane Library as covering all trials — it maintains **CENTRAL** but not every intervention trial is registered there, and it is not a substitute for Medline.

blocks.title: Hierarchy of Evidence (Highest to Lowest)
rows: Systematic review of several double-blind RCTs
One or more large double-blind RCTs

blocks.text: A commonly examined ranking (highest to lowest robustness): meta-analysis > systematic review > **RCT** > non-randomised trial > cohort study > case-control study.

Reporting-guideline map: **CONSORT** for RCTs; **QUOROM** (an early standard, since superseded by **PRISMA**) for meta-analyses of RCTs; **PRISMA** for systematic reviews; **STROBE** for observational studies (cohort/case-control/cross-sectional); **STARD** for diagnostic-accuracy studies; **MOOSE** for meta-analyses of observational studies; **COREQ** for qualitative research (interviews/focus groups).

blocks.text: **NICE** is the independent **UK** body that produces national consensus guidance in three areas: public health, health technologies, and clinical practice.
The Delphi method is an iterative, multistage group-facilitation technique used to transform expert opinion into a group consensus, commonly used to develop treatment guidelines.

sections.title: 3. Diagnostic Test Accuracy — Sensitivity, Specificity & Predictive Values

blocks.text: Diagnostic accuracy = all correct hits / total observations; this is a coarser measure that is generally superseded by the finer measures of sensitivity and specificity.

Serial (sequential) testing — a second test only given if the first is positive — increases the specificity but decreases the sensitivity of the combined battery. Simultaneous (parallel) testing does the opposite: sensitivity rises, specificity falls, versus either test alone.

blocks.title: Diagnostic accuracy — core formulas
rows: Ability to correctly identify true positives among the diseased
Ability to correctly identify true negatives among the well
**LR** x pre-test odds (pre-test odds derived from prevalence)
Used to get post-test probability = odds / (odds + 1)

sources.file: question_bank/EBM/EMIs Evidence Based Medicine_ Attempt review.pdf
question_bank/EBM/EMIs Evidence Based Medicine_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.forTopic: Using sensitivity/specificity to rule disease in or out
expansion: SnNout — a test with high SeNsitivity, when Negative, helps rule **OUT** disease
SpPin — a test with high SPecificity, when Positive, helps rule **IN** disease

blocks.text: **EMI** trap: distinguishing 'the prevalence of disease among test-positives' (= **PPV** = **TP**/total positive) from 'how likely a positive result is given disease' (= likelihood ratio, sensitivity/(1-specificity)) — these produce different-looking but easily confused fractions from the same 2x2 table.

source.file: question_bank/EBM/EMIs Evidence Based Medicine_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Higher disease prevalence in the tested population raises positive predictive value (**PPV**) for the same test, with the gain plateauing at higher prevalence levels; **PPV** rises and **NPV** falls as prevalence increases.

Sensitivity, specificity and the likelihood ratio (**LR**+) are properties of the test itself and are not affected by disease prevalence in the population tested — only **PPV** and **NPV** are prevalence-dependent.

Lowering a diagnostic cut-off (e.g. from 21 to 14 units of alcohol) increases false positives (raises sensitivity, lowers specificity); raising the cut-off does the reverse. For a serious disease with an effective early treatment, the cut-off should be set to minimise false negatives even at the cost of more false positives.

Raising a diagnostic cut-off from 3 to 4 on the **CAGE** reduces sensitivity but leaves specificity **UNCHANGED** in the sourced worked example — candidates often assume specificity must rise whenever sensitivity falls.
The best likelihood-ratio cut-off is not necessarily the one that maximises sensitivity or specificity individually — it is typically the central/median cut-off where the two trade off best.

Post-test odds = likelihood ratio x pre-test odds, where pre-test odds are derived from prevalence (the pre-test probability); post-test probability is then odds/(odds+1). Example: sensitivity ==80%==, specificity ==90%==, prevalence ==10%== -> **LR**+ = 8, post-test odds = 8/9, post-test probability approx 0.47.
Worked example of Bayesian updating: pre-test probability 1/4 (odds 1/3), **LR**+ = 9.5 (from sensitivity ==95%==/specificity ==90%==) -> post-test odds = 3.16 -> post-test probability approx 0.75.

blocks.subtopic: Bayesian reasoning beyond basic post-test probability
blocks.note: The sourced questions only cover the mechanics of converting prevalence -> pre-test odds -> post-test odds/probability via a likelihood ratio. There is no coverage in this question bank of Bayesian priors more generally, decision-curve analysis, or how clinical judgement should combine with these calculations in practice.

blocks.text: The single most important methodological safeguard when validating a new test against a 'gold standard' is that the two tests must be applied independently of each other.

A Receiver Operator Characteristic (**ROC**) curve plots sensitivity (true positive rate) on the y-axis against 1-specificity (false positive rate) on the x-axis; it is used to select the best cut-off and to compare two or more diagnostic instruments.

The area under the **ROC** curve (**AUC**) represents overall test accuracy; an **AUC** of 0.5 means the test cannot discriminate diseased from non-diseased any better than a coin toss — this is the performance of the diagonal 'line of no discrimination'.
**AUC** = 0.5 on an **ROC** curve is a trap for assuming any reported **AUC** implies good test performance — 0.5 means the test performs no better than chance (the diagonal line).
1-specificity, plotted on the **ROC** x-axis, is the false positive rate (since true negatives + false positives = ==100%== of non-diseased cases).
The best trade-off cut-off point sits at the 'elbow'/knee of the **ROC** curve, where sensitivity and specificity are jointly optimised even though neither is individually maximal.

sections.title: 5. Case-Control Studies — Odds Ratio, Bias & What Cannot Be Calculated

blocks.text: Odds ratio (**OR**) is the cross-product ratio (a x d)/(b x c) from a 2x2 table; **OR** cannot take a negative value. Worked example: 3 of 2000 cases and 1 of 2000 controls exposed -> **OR** = (3x1999)/(1x1997) approx 3.

Relative risk **CANNOT** be calculated from a case-control study — only from incidence data (cohort/prospective designs); the retrospective design does not distinguish new from old cases, so only odds ratio can be produced.
Case-control studies cannot establish a temporal association between exposure and outcome (though dose-response patterns and confidence intervals for the **OR** can still be derived).

blocks.forTopic: What a case-control study cannot give you
blocks.mnemonic: The RAT stays out of case-control
expansion: R — Relative risk cannot be calculated
A — Attributable/population risk cannot be calculated
T — Temporal sequence between exposure and outcome cannot be established

blocks.title: What each observational design can and cannot calculate
rows: Odds ratio, dose-response pattern, **CI** for the **OR**
Relative risk, incidence, temporal association, true population prevalence (unless representatively sampled)
Odds ratio, plus temporal association (register data recorded prospectively)
Still cannot rule out confounding (remains observational)
Sensitivity, specificity, **PPV**/**NPV** for the sample studied
True population prevalence, unless the sample is representative

blocks.text: Given the same case/control exposure counts, one cannot determine true population prevalence from a convenience-sampled diagnostic/case-control dataset — this requires a genuinely representative sample.
Case-control design is the most efficient choice when the disease under study is rare, even after exposure — a cohort design would need an impractically large sample to observe enough rare events.

A nested case-control study identifies cases from a defined, prospectively followed cohort/register (e.g. **GPRD**) and samples matched non-cases from that same cohort using incidence density sampling (time-matched to the case's incidence date); this reduces recall and selection bias relative to a classic case-control design.

Despite being analysed retrospectively, a nested case-control study **CAN** support temporal-association claims because the underlying exposure/outcome data were recorded prospectively on the register before the analysis was done.

Nested case-control design is a trap for assuming all case-control designs share the same weaknesses: because the underlying register data were recorded prospectively, temporal association **CAN** be inferred here, unlike a classic case-control study.

Even a carefully matched, register-based nested case-control design remains an observational design — confounding by an unmeasured third variable remains a threat to validity that cannot be experimentally excluded.

From a case-control association alone, one cannot infer a causal relationship (e.g. 'antipsychotics cause hip fractures') — only the strength of association (**OR**, with **CI**) can be inferred; equally, no prescriptive clinical guideline can be derived from such cross-sectional/case-control work alone.

Multiple linear regression can give unreliable/unstable significance estimates for individual predictors when two included independent variables are highly correlated with each other (multicollinearity) — they compete for statistical significance rather than acting as independent predictors.

Multicollinearity trap: when two independent variables in a multiple regression are highly correlated, individual predictors can appear falsely non-significant — this is not a sign the whole model or the outcome measure is invalid.

A low absolute prevalence of the exposure among cases (e.g. very few schizophrenia patients in a given cancer subgroup) increases the risk of a Type 2 error — a true association may be missed unless the sample is large enough.

**EMI** trap: the same raw 2x2 count table produces different valid statistics depending on whether it is labelled case-control, cohort, or cross-sectional — incidence rate and relative risk are only valid for the cohort framing, odds ratio for case-control, and prevalence for cross-sectional.

items.text: Relative risk is a classic case-control trap: it cannot be calculated from a case-control study (only odds ratio can), because retrospective sampling does not identify incidence.
Case-control studies are repeatedly tested as unable to establish temporal association between exposure and outcome, even when dose-response and **OR** confidence intervals are available.
Interpreting an **OR** of 5 from a case-control study as if it were a relative risk ('5 times greater risk') is wrong — the correct phrasing is in terms of odds, not risk.

'Point prevalence of the disease in the population' cannot be answered from a diagnostic-accuracy study built on a convenience (non-representative) sample of cases and controls — a common trap is assuming the case:control ratio approximates population prevalence.

sections.title: 6. Cohort Studies — Attributable Risk & Population Impact

blocks.text: Relative risk equal to or below 1.0 means no positive association between exposure and outcome — the risk in exposed persons equals (or is below) the risk in non-exposed persons.

blocks.title: Cohort Studies — Attributable Risk Formulas
rows: Pe(**RR**-1) / [1+Pe(**RR**-1)], Pe = proportion of population exposed

blocks.text: If an exposure has an attributable risk of ==100%== for a disease, this means all incident cases of that disease are the result of that single exposure — a situation that is rarely, if ever, seen in practice.
Randomisation balances known and unknown confounders between groups at baseline; lack of randomisation (e.g. using self-selected volunteers) is a serious threat to external validity/generalisability.

The similarity of baseline characteristics between randomised groups is most likely attributable to randomisation itself, not to blinding or to intention-to-treat analysis (which act at later stages of the trial).

Intention-to-treat (**ITT**) analysis includes every randomised patient in the group to which they were originally allocated, regardless of adherence or early 'cure' — omitting non-adherers undermines the unbiased comparison that randomisation provides.
Even when more patients drop out of one arm than another, an **ITT** analysis (analysing all patients per their original allocation) is the correct approach to preserve the value of randomisation.

Crossover trials are not subject to confounding by age, sex or other personal characteristics (each patient acts as their own control) and need fewer patients than parallel-group trials, but they are unsuitable for irreversible endpoints such as cure or death.

n-of-1 trials are most useful when RCTs show a treatment is effective on average but a substantial proportion of patients do not respond, leaving doubt about whether this particular patient will benefit.

n-of-1 trials are not appropriate to evaluate a treatment with only weak evidence for a potentially curative effect on a long-standing condition — and are impractical when a condition might fully resolve within the observation period.
A placebo (or active) run-in phase before randomisation is used to improve compliance — it can weed out non-compliers, wash out previous treatment, and establish a stable baseline before allocation.
The odd/even last-digit-of-date-of-birth method of allocation is a quasi-randomisation technique and is the least adequate method of treatment allocation in a clinical trial.

Cluster-randomised trials (randomising groups such as nursing-home units rather than individuals) reduce the effective sample size relative to individual randomisation of the same total N — higher power for a given N is achievable without cluster sampling.

Cluster-randomised trials need **MORE** participants than an individually-randomised trial of the same total N to achieve equivalent power, because intracluster correlation reduces the effective sample size.

Intracluster correlation is the proportion of total outcome variability attributable to between-cluster (rather than within-cluster) differences; a high value means participants within a cluster behave like a single observational unit, shrinking the effective sample size toward the number of clusters.
Equivalence trials require the largest sample size of all **RCT** types, since demonstrating a near-zero effect-size difference between treatments is statistically the hardest target to prove.

Equivalence trials are a trap for assuming smaller effect sizes need smaller samples — in fact equivalence trials (near-zero difference to demonstrate) require the **LARGEST** sample sizes of all **RCT** types.

Repeated administration of the same or a similar test (e.g. a pre/post **CPD** quiz) can itself produce score gains through a repeat-testing/practice effect — this must be considered before crediting an intervention with the improvement.

Patients in the control arms of RCTs tend to do better than similar non-trial patients for reasons besides the specific intervention (a 'trial participation effect') — better clinician input, favourable selection, protocol adherence and a placebo/participation effect, but **NOT** simply higher medication potency.

sections.title: 8. Interpreting RCT Results — NNT, ARR, RRR & Confidence Intervals

blocks.title: Treatment-effect measures — NNT, NNH, ARR, RRR, RR, OR

sources.file: question_bank/EBM/EMIs Evidence Based Medicine_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **ARR** (absolute risk reduction) = |**CER** - **EER**|. Worked example: **chlorpromazine** relapse ==45%== vs new drug ==50%== -> **ARR** = 0.05 (the new drug is actually worse here, but **ARR** is reported as the absolute difference).
**NNT** = 1/**ARR**. Worked example: drug A 20/200 deaths vs placebo 25/225 deaths over 3 years -> **ARR** = 1/90 -> **NNT** = 90 to prevent one death.

**NNH** (number needed to harm) is calculated the same way as **NNT** but for an adverse outcome: **NNH** = 1/**ARR** for the harmful event. Worked example: **NNH** = 60 for suicidal acts on an antidepressant, used to back-calculate the actual event count in the treated arm (70 of 600).
**RR** = **EER**/**CER**. Worked example: drug A 20/200 vs placebo 25/225 deaths -> **RR** = 0.9.
**RRR** = 1 - **RR** (equivalently **ARR**/**CER**). Worked example continuing above: **RRR** = 1 - 0.9 = 0.1 (==10%==).

**RRR** figures are usually far larger-looking than the corresponding **ARR**/risk-difference, which can make results seem more impressive than they are clinically — e.g. a ==50%== **RRR** may represent only a ==2%==->==1%== absolute drop.

**RRR** figures are deliberately tested because they look far more impressive than the corresponding **ARR** (e.g. a '==50%== **RRR**' framing can hide a ==2%==->==1%== absolute change) — always convert back to **ARR**/**NNT** before judging clinical significance.

Assuming a constant **RRR**, **NNT** is inversely proportional to the baseline (control) event rate: a higher-risk population needs fewer patients treated per event prevented, and vice versa; **NNT** is also inversely related to **RRR** itself.

For relative risk reduction (**RRR**) and other difference-based statistics, the null value is zero — a ==95%== **CI** must not cross zero to be statistically significant. For ratio-based statistics (**RR**, **OR**), the null value is 1.
If a trial's exact p-value for a treatment effect is 0.05, the lower bound of the ==95%== **CI** for the relative risk is likely to sit right at 1.
Increasing sample size while event rates stay the same does not change the point estimate of **RR** or **RRR** — it narrows the confidence interval around that same estimate, it does not shift it.

Increasing an **RCT**'s sample size while event rates stay identical is a trap for assuming the point estimate of **RR**/**RRR** changes — it only narrows the confidence interval, the point estimate stays the same.

A wide ==95%== **CI** for **RRR** spanning both harm and benefit (e.g. -==28%== to +==49%==) means the trial has not actually resolved whether to offer the treatment, even if the point estimate looks favourable.

For an apparently 'negative' trial (p>0.05), check the upper bound of the **CI**: if it still contains an important treatment benefit, a real beneficial effect cannot be ruled out — only if the upper bound excludes any important benefit is the trial 'definitively negative'.
A trial with p>0.05 ('negative') is not automatically proof of no effect — check whether the upper **CI** bound still contains an important benefit before calling it 'definitively negative'.
Subgroup analysis results are more trustworthy when the subgroup hypothesis was specified before the study began, rather than generated after seeing the data.

Composite endpoints (e.g. death + **MI** + heart failure combined) reduce the required sample size and follow-up duration, but should not be used on the assumption that patients weight each component outcome equally — they usually do not.

A surrogate/substitute endpoint is an easily measurable proxy used instead of the true patient-relevant outcome (e.g. a biomarker instead of survival); surrogates are attractive for feasibility but can be misleading. Activities-of-daily-living scores in a dementia trial are an example of a genuine (non-surrogate) patient-relevant outcome, not a surrogate.
The hazard ratio is essentially a relative risk weighted for the number of patients at risk over time in a survival analysis — useful when timing of onset, not just total count, matters.
The most common reason RCTs are stopped early is the appearance of a large treatment effect that seems unlikely to be due to chance — not usually cost-saving or loss of investigator interest.

Random error has a larger relative influence on the results of smaller studies (affecting reliability/reproducibility), whereas bias affects validity independent of sample size — a biased study can still be highly reproducible yet still wrong.

sections.title: 9. Meta-Analysis — Heterogeneity & Choice of Statistical Model

blocks.text: Statistical heterogeneity is formally tested with Cochran's Q test and the I-squared statistic, and can be explored visually via forest plots, Galbraith plots and L'Abbe plots — using a second independent reviewer to select studies addresses selection bias, not heterogeneity, and is the odd one out among heterogeneity-assessment options.

A significant (low p-value) Cochran's Q result means the null hypothesis of 'all variability due to chance' is rejected, i.e. statistical heterogeneity is present; the test is sensitive to study sample sizes, so it can fail to flag true heterogeneity in small studies and can flag trivial heterogeneity in very large ones.

A significant Cochran's Q test is sensitive to the number/size of included studies: it may fail to flag true heterogeneity when studies are small, and flag trivial heterogeneity when studies are very large — don't treat its p-value as definitive on its own.
A fixed-effect model assumes every included study is estimating the same true effect, with only within-study sampling variation causing observed differences (i.e. 'differences are due to chance').

Choosing between fixed-effect and random-effects models is about the **ASSUMPTION** of a single true effect vs accepting heterogeneity — not primarily about differences in methodological quality between studies.

A random-effects model is used specifically because heterogeneity exists between studies; it accepts that each study may be estimating a different underlying effect and incorporates between-study variance, generally widening the pooled confidence interval.

The Galbraith plot displays each study as a point (z-score/effect-size-over-**SE** on the y-axis vs 1/**SE** on the x-axis) around a central regression line; points falling outside a 2-**SD** band around that line are considered outliers, and points near the zero-line show no effect.

sections.title: 10. Meta-Analysis — Effect Size, Data Synthesis & Publication Bias

blocks.text: For dichotomous outcomes, effect size in meta-analyses is usually expressed as odds ratio or relative risk; likelihood ratio is a diagnostic-test measure and is **NOT** generally used to express meta-analytic effect size.
When individual studies measured a continuous outcome on the **SAME** rating scale, results can be combined directly using the weighted mean difference.

When individual studies measured a continuous outcome on **DIFFERENT** rating scales (e.g. **HAM-D** vs **BDI** for depression), results must first be standardised via the standardised mean difference (**SMD**, e.g. Cohen's d = difference in means divided by pooled **SD**) before pooling.

If a study's mean is smaller than its standard deviation, the underlying data are likely skewed — the researcher should consider a log transform or dichotomising the outcome rather than pooling the raw **SD**-based statistic.

When an included study's mean outcome is smaller than its own standard deviation, this signals skewed data that undermines simple **SD**-based pooling — a trap for assuming any continuous outcome can be pooled with a mean/**SD** approach.

Failsafe N is Rosenthal's estimate of the number of additional null/negative unpublished studies ('file-drawer' studies) that would be needed to reduce a significant meta-analytic result to non-significance.

A funnel plot (study size plotted against effect size/**OR**) is used to detect publication bias via asymmetry; the confidence interval of the pooled effect size is **NOT** a valid way to detect publication bias, since it is simply a function of total sample size and number of trials.

The confidence interval of a meta-analysis's pooled effect size is explicitly **NOT** a valid method for detecting publication bias (that needs a funnel plot or failsafe N) — a common distractor in publication-bias questions.

blocks.title: The 4 Basic Steps of a Meta-Analysis
Typical Stages of a Systematic Review (Higgins 2008)

blocks.text: A systematic review search strategy must include unpublished studies and papers in all languages, not just English peer-reviewed publications — restricting to peer-reviewed English papers risks publication/language bias.

A risk ratio (**RR**) of 1 indicates no difference between groups; a risk ratio below 1 does **NOT** by itself mean 'no difference' — its statistical significance still depends on whether its **CI** excludes 1.

**NNT** can be derived from a meta-analysis's pooled absolute risk difference exactly as from a single trial. Worked example: **risperidone** vs **haloperidol** for **PANSS** improvement, pooled **ARR** = 0.125 -> **NNT** = 8, with ==95%== **CI** for **NNT** = 7 to 10 (calculated from the **CI** bounds of the **ARR**).

sections.title: 11. Forest Plots, L'Abbe Plots & Other EBM Graphs

blocks.text: A forest plot ('blobbogram') represents each study as a block/square at its point estimate, with a horizontal line showing its confidence interval; the size of the square reflects the study's weight in the pooled estimate. Forest plots are produced by meta-analytic (secondary) research.

expansion: S — Square size shows the study's Weight in the pooled estimate
W — Width of the horizontal line shows imprecision (wider = less precise)
A — Arrowhead means the **CI** extends beyond the plotted axis (very imprecise)
P — Pooled diamond/summary line at the bottom gives the overall effect

blocks.text: Heterogeneity, by definition, cannot be calculated for a single stand-alone trial in a forest plot — it only applies to the pooled set of studies.

Precision of a study's (or the pooled) estimate is reflected by the width of its horizontal line in a forest plot — narrower lines mean more precise results; an arrowhead on the line means the **CI** extends beyond the plotted axis range (a highly imprecise result).

blocks.title: Recognising common EBM graph types
rows: Point estimate + **CI** per study (block size = weight)
Experimental event rate vs control event rate, one circle per study
Visualising heterogeneity in raw event rates across studies
Standardised effect (z-score) vs 1/**SE**, one point per study
Choosing a diagnostic cut-off / comparing tests (**AUC** = accuracy)
Willingness-to-pay threshold vs probability **ICER** is below it

blocks.text: An L'Abbe plot plots each individual study as a circle with the experimental event rate (**EER**) on one axis and control event rate (**CER**) on the other; circle size typically represents study sample size (colour/shading can indicate subgroup, e.g. hospital vs primary-care setting). Studies above the line of equality favour the experimental treatment.
**CONSORT** recommends including a participant flow diagram for RCTs, and such diagrams are strongly recommended to always show the attrition/dropout rate.

A cost-effectiveness acceptability curve plots a range of willingness-to-pay thresholds against the probability that the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (**ICER**) falls below that threshold — it visualises statistical uncertainty in cost-effectiveness estimates.

A scatterplot of country-level (ecological) data, such as income inequality vs prevalence of mental illness across nations, risks the ecological fallacy if used to infer relationships at the individual level.

Plotting cumulative incidence (via Kaplan-Meier estimates) separately for each birth cohort demonstrates the combined effect of both age and calendar/birth year on incidence of a diagnosis — useful for showing trend-over-time alongside age effects.

sections.title: 12. Survival Analysis — Kaplan-Meier, Log-Rank & Cox Regression

blocks.text: Survival methods measure 'time to an event' (e.g. discharge, death) and do not require a near-normal distribution, unlike the parametric assumptions of a t-test or **ANOVA**; they are preferable to a chi-square approach, which would lose information by dichotomising continuous time data.

In a Kaplan-Meier plot, the y-axis shows the proportion of subjects who have **NOT** yet reached the outcome of interest, and the x-axis shows time; plotting the y-axis on a log scale can make the curve look deceptively linear.

The log-rank test assesses the effect of a single categorical variable on survival; Cox proportional hazards regression is needed to assess continuous variables (or multiple variables simultaneously), and assumes the hazard ratio is constant over time.

Cox regression allows the effect of one variable on survival to be estimated while adjusting for others, distinguishing a variable's independent effect from one that is only associated with survival via another variable.

The median survival time is the time point at which the survival curve reaches ==50%==; if the curve is right-censored before reaching that point (follow-up ends too early), median survival time cannot be determined.

blocks.note: Only 6 questions were sourced for this sub-bank, and all of them concern survival-analysis mechanics (Kaplan-Meier, log-rank test, Cox regression) rather than prognosis-specific study design issues such as inception cohorts, prognostic-factor selection, clinical prediction rules, or prognosis-specific biases (e.g. lead-time or length-time bias). Cross-check against a core clinical epidemiology text for these.

blocks.text: Deleting items that show significant misfit to a Rasch measurement model (e.g. from the 14-item to the 7-item Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Well-Being Scale) improves construct validity, since the remaining items fit the underlying construct model better.

A shortened scale can lose some face validity (a more restricted view of the construct) even while gaining ease-of-use, brevity, and reduced confounding by gender/age bias present in the deleted items.
Test-retest reliability is the method used to demonstrate that an instrument's scores remain stable over a defined period (e.g. 2 weeks).

A summed interval-scale score (e.g. a short well-being scale) does not have meaningful physical units, even though it permits parametric comparison (t-test) or non-parametric comparison (Mann-Whitney U) depending on whether normality assumptions hold.

The most important single component in developing a clinical guideline is having a systematically reviewed evidence base on which recommendations are built — even though guidance also incorporates value judgements and resource availability.

It is **NOT** appropriate to prepare guideline recommendations irrespective of local resources — resource availability should modify a recommended action even when the underlying evidence base is strong.

Steps in producing a treatment recommendation: define the decision, specify the possible outcomes, use available evidence to link options to outcomes, incorporate value judgements, then adjust for local resource availability — this explains why guidance for the same evidence base can differ between countries (e.g. **NICE** vs French/Canadian dementia-drug guidance).

Guidelines are most effectively implemented when developed by those who will use them, disseminated through a specific educational intervention, and reinforced by patient-specific reminders during consultations (e.g. filed in the notes).
The most effective single measure for getting clinicians to apply a new guideline in practice is using patient-specific reminders at the point of clinical contact.

blocks.note: The **GRADE** approach to grading quality of evidence and strength of recommendations is never mentioned anywhere in the 239 sourced questions, despite being a standard **EBM**/guideline topic. Recommend reviewing the **GRADE** handbook or **NICE**'s methods manual directly.

Only 5 questions were sourced for this sub-bank. Coverage is limited to general principles of guideline development and implementation (evidence + values + resources, Delphi consensus); it does not cover formal recommendation-strength grading (e.g. **GRADE** strong/weak) or guideline-appraisal instruments (**AGREE** **II**).

Cross-check this guide against a dedicated critical appraisal / **EBM** textbook (e.g. Greenhalgh's 'How to Read a Paper', the **CASP** checklists, or the RCPsych Paper B syllabus statistics/research-methods chapter) before relying on it alone.

blocks.note: Although **RCT**/guideline quality is discussed conceptually throughout this question bank, none of the standard named critical-appraisal instruments (**CASP** tools, Jadad scale, **AGREE** **II** for guidelines, PEDro) are referenced in any sourced explanation. Check a **CASP** course or a core **EBM** textbook for these instruments specifically.
